name: Yamdena
confidence_why: Mettler & Mettler 1990, the Indonesian grammar by Rumyaru, Mettler & Mettler 1999 and the much older Drabbe 1926 all put default stress on the penultimate syllable of the root and differ only over how many morphological and grammatical constructions push it onto the final syllable, so the penultimate placement stands while the 'strict' qualifier overstates what any of them says.

new_statements.quote: §32. De klemtoon valt altijd op den wortel en niet op den uitgang. Alleen om grammatikale redenen kan hij in stammen met gesloten wortel en gesloten uitgang verspringen op den uitgang. De gevallen, waarin dat gebeurt, zullen we hier achtereenvolgens behandelen. [...] §33. Als een stamwoord als werkwoord gebruikt wordt, en zoowel een overgankelijke als een onovergankelijke beteekenis kan hebben, verschuift de klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep, wanneer het geen voorwerp bij zich heeft [...] §38. In het Zuiderdialect blijft in het meervoud de klemtoon op den wortel; in het Noorderdialect verschuift hij naar den meervoudsuitgang ar.
new_statements.translation: §32. The stress always falls on the root and not on the ending. Only for grammatical reasons can it, in stems with a closed root and a closed ending, jump to the ending. The cases in which that happens we treat here one by one. [...] §33. When a stem word is used as a verb and can have both a transitive and an intransitive meaning, the stress shifts to the last syllable when it has no object with it [...] §38. In the Southern dialect the stress stays on the root in the plural; in the Northern dialect it shifts to the plural ending ar.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate rule for unmodified words (root = penult of a bare stem) but adds a whole set of grammatically conditioned shifts to the final syllable, a north/south dialect difference in plurals, and stressed possessive suffixes. It also implies stress can be grammatically contrastive (transitive vs intransitive readings), which sits uneasily with the 1999 pedoman's 'not phonemic'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress sits on the root (wortel), i.e. the penultimate syllable of a bare stem (stems being root + ending in Drabbe's analysis), and moves to the final syllable (the ending) only under grammatical conditions: an object-less (intransitive/'neuter') use of a verb that can be transitive (nmálip jak 'he laughs at me' vs nmalíp 'he laughs'), a noun used as a real locative (jakti dlás 'I go to the forest' vs sirár dlas silai 'they have much forest'), a noun after the negator to 'none', a predicative adjective with an adjectival prefix, and (Northern dialect only) the plural ending -ar; possessive suffixes that contain a vowel are always stressed, vowel-less ones (ng, m, n) leave stress on the root.
new_statements.exceptions: Stems that are never transitive keep root stress (tanoek: i natanoek 'he speaks'); relational nouns (betrekkings-zelfst. nw.) always keep root stress; a stem used as a plain adjective never changes stress; in the plural the Southern dialect keeps root stress while the Northern dialect shifts to -ar; possessive suffixes with a vowel (limnindar, limmir/limnir) take the stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Drabbe 1926 distinguishes a Noorderdialect and a Zuiderdialect of Yamdena; in the plural the Southern dialect keeps root stress while the Northern dialect shifts stress to -ar (§38). The 1999 pedoman names the same split (Nus Das 'upper island' north vs Nus Bab 'lower island' south) and its plural examples (bulnár, aswár) follow the Northern pattern; the Mettlers worked in Atubul Raya, Ilngei and Sangliat Krawain. The Lund corpus landing page treats Yamdena (jmd) as one language, 30,000 speakers, Tanimbar Islands.

new_statements.quote: 1.5.1. Tekanan kata pada dasarnya. Setiap bentuk kata dasar/akar kata yang belum dimodifikasi, tekanan kata selalu jatuh pada suku kedua dari akhir kata. Tekanan kata tersebut tidak fonemis dan tidak perlu ditulis. [...] Kata-kata yang bersuku satu saja, tekanan kata di atas suku satu itu. Prefiks persona (atau prefiks yang menyatakan subyek) yang terdapat dalam kata kerja atau kata sifat berprefiks tidak terkena tekanan kata. [...] 1.5.2. Pergeseran tekanan kata tidak terjadi apabila afiks plural (penunjuk jamak) "-ar" ditambahkan pada akar kata yang berakhir dengan "-e" [...] Sebaliknya, bila afiks jamak tersebut ditambahkan pada akar kata yang berakhir dengan bunyi yang bukan "e", [...] Tekanan kata akan berpindah ke afiks jamak.
new_statements.translation: 1.5.1. Word stress basically. In every unmodified base word/root, word stress always falls on the second syllable from the end of the word. This word stress is not phonemic and need not be written. [...] In monosyllabic words the stress is on that one syllable. The person prefix (the prefix expressing the subject) found on prefixed verbs or adjectives does not receive word stress. [...] 1.5.2. No shift of word stress occurs when the plural affix '-ar' is added to a root ending in '-e' [...] Conversely, when that plural affix is added to a root ending in a sound other than 'e', [...] the word stress moves to the plural affix.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Penultimate stress on every unmodified root (léte, katútun, ásu, léndan); non-phonemic and unwritten; monosyllables stressed; subject prefixes never stressed (kumín, muflá, kufínau); the plural affix -ar takes the stress when added to a root not ending in -e (búlan > bulnár, ásu > aswár, sóri > soryár) but not after -e roots (léte > létar, dóle > dólar).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts to the plural affix -ar except for roots in -e; person prefixes are extrametrical.
new_statements.identity_note: Drabbe 1926 distinguishes a Noorderdialect and a Zuiderdialect of Yamdena; in the plural the Southern dialect keeps root stress while the Northern dialect shifts stress to -ar (§38). The 1999 pedoman names the same split (Nus Das 'upper island' north vs Nus Bab 'lower island' south) and its plural examples (bulnár, aswár) follow the Northern pattern; the Mettlers worked in Atubul Raya, Ilngei and Sangliat Krawain. The Lund corpus landing page treats Yamdena (jmd) as one language, 30,000 speakers, Tanimbar Islands.

readall_conflicts: Neither listed work could be read (SIL 94080 is 'Not Available Online'; the Lund corpus files need a login), so no new conflict arises from them. Between the two on-disk descriptions: Rumyaru, Mettler & Mettler 1999 give plain penultimate stress on unmodified roots and call it non-phonemic, while Drabbe 1926 frames stress as 'always on the root' with grammatically conditioned shifts to the final syllable (object-less verbs, locative nouns, predicative adjectives, nouns after to, Northern-dialect plural -ar, vowel-bearing possessive suffixes) and gives minimal pairs where the shift carries meaning (nmálip jak 'he laughs at me' vs nmalíp 'he laughs'), i.e. stress that is grammatically contrastive. The two agree on the default position and on the plural -ar shift; they differ on whether the shifted stress is contrastive, and Drabbe ties the plural shift to the Northern dialect only.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every quoted sentence is verbatim in the held Mettler & Mettler 1990 scan at pp.44-45. The source is the right one (only dedicated phonology; endorsed as such by Visser 2024, also held). But the classification 'fixed-strict, penult, domain word' over-reads it. Mettler 1990 itself says stress is penult OF THE ROOT, that personal prefixes are never stressed (ku-'min, mu-'fla = final stress on disyllabic words), and that plural -ar takes the stress after non-e-final roots (lend'nar, as'war, sor'yar = final stress); §7.3 adds shifts 'to the ultimate syllable' from vowel deletion and phrase stress, 'in particular for verbs'. Rumyaru & Mettler 1999 §1.5 (downloaded now) repeats all of this with accent-marked forms (kumín, muflá, bulnár, aswár). sources.quote: §1.5.1: 'Setiap bentuk kata dasar/akar kata yang belum dimodifikasi, tekanan kata selalu jatuh pada suku kedua dari akhir kata. Tekanan kata tersebut tidak fonemis' (in every unmodified base/root, stress always falls on the second syllable from the end; not phonemic): léte, katútun, ásu, léndan. Person prefixes on verbs/adjectives are never stressed: kumín 'I stay', muflá 'you run', mimpán, mamín, raflá, kufínau. §1.5.2: no shift when plural -ar is added to e-final roots (léte > létar, dóle > dólar); otherwise 'Tekanan kata akan berpindah ke afiks jamak' (stress moves to the plural affix): búl
